answer_raw.explanation: ROOT CAUSE: The new well upgrade introduced water with elevated bicarbonate/alkalinity. As this water is applied, bicarbonate accumulates in the root zone and drives up rhizosphere pH. At high pH, iron and manganese become insoluble and unavailable to the plant, causing interveinal chlorosis (the characteristic symptom of Fe/Mn deficiency) and triggering the ~30% yield decline. This also explains why routine soil and tissue panels read 'within range' — total elemental levels can appear adequate even when plant-available fractions are locked out by pH. EVIDENCE: (1) No acidifier + low irrigation = near-zero yield (exp3: +0.8). (2) No acidifier + high irrigation = strongly negative yield (exp4: −13.6) — more water = more bicarbonate loading = worse outcome, ruling out under-watering as the cause. (3) Acidifier + high irrigation = partial recovery (exp5: +19.0), showing acidifier counteracts bicarbonate but high irrigation volume overwhelms it. (4) Acidifier dose-response at low irrigation: yield peaks near dose=65 (exp9: +30.7), then declines at dose=100 (exp8: +20.3), confirming a true optimum rather than monotonic response. (5) A 2D quadratic model (R²=0.997) across all 7 interventions confirms the optimum at irrigation=25, acidifier≈63–65. DECISIVE TEST: Experiment 4 vs. 3 showed more water alone makes things dramatically worse (−13.6 vs. +0.8), falsifying the 'under-watering' and 'nitrogen shortfall' hypotheses. The dose-response curve of the acidifier (rising then falling yield) proves it is acting on a real chemical equilibrium (pH), not merely a confounded signal. RECOMMENDED FIX: Reduce irrigation rate to the lower setting (25) to minimize bicarbonate loading, and apply SoilAcidifier at dose 65 to neutralize accumulated bicarbonate and restore rhizosphere pH to the range where Fe/Mn solubility supports full crop demand. Best observed yield: 30.7 (vs. baseline ~0.8 without intervention), representing full recovery and more.
